paper.title: Robots and immigration
paper.journal: Journal of Economic Behavior and Organization
paper.code_data_availability: Data availability statement (p. 18), verbatim: 'The data that has been used is confidential.' No DST project number is given. …

registers.name_in_paper: Integrated Database for Labor Market Research (IDA)
Firm-Integrated Database for Labor Market Research (FIDA)

registers.role: outcome: robot adoption measured from firm-level imports
variables_mentioned: HS 847989 other machines and mechanical appliances having individual functions

registers.role: validation of the robot-adoption measure and an alternative outcome
variables_mentioned: reported robot usage in the previous year

linkages: workers in IDA linked to their employers in FIRM through FIDA using a unique identifier
firm-level robot imports from the Foreign Trade Statistics Register linked to the employer-employee data by firm identifier
firms linked to municipalities; for multi-establishment companies the immigration variable and its instrument are an employment-weighted average across establishment locations
VITA survey responses linked to the register data by firm identifier

sample.universe: Danish private-sector firms with more than 50 employees that last at least 12 years, 1995-2019, in 94 municipalities, linked to the universe of Danish workers
sample.unit_of_observation: firm-year (municipality-year and worker-year for the mechanism tables)
selection_rules: start from the merged employer-employee dataset: 3,674,768 observations, 14,650 robot observations (Table A.1)
drop wholesale machinery firms: 3,610,730 observations, 10,973 robot observations
drop robot integrators (six-digit industry codes from Humlum, 2021): 3,536,697 / 8,359
drop short-duration firms (active less than 12 years): 62,262 / 2,561
drop 3 outlier municipalities that never experienced a robot adoption: 61,007 / 2,561
firms that export robots are also dropped
sample.n_observations: 61,007 firm-year observations in the baseline regressions
sample.n_individuals: 5,105 firms (Table 2); the text describes an unbalanced panel of approximately 6,000 firms; worker-level regressions use 48,228,392 worker-year observations

construction_notes: robots are defined by HS product codes 847950 and 847989; the two categories are used jointly because 847950 alone does not match IFR robot-shipment statistics
robot imports and robot adoptions are used interchangeably; the measure is validated against the VITA survey (false-positive rate 4.7%, false-negative rate 70.6%, accuracy 83.3%, survey-weighted)
trade and accounting variables are in real Danish kroner using 2015 as the base year; 1 Danish krone is approximately 0.15 US dollar
the immigration variable for multi-establishment companies is an employment-weighted average across establishment locations, and a multi-establishment dummy is controlled for throughout
routine occupations are those with a routine-task share of at least 70%, using Mihaylov and Tijdens (2019) following Autor and Dorn (2013)
low-skill workers are workers without completed secondary education; blue-collar workers are those in DISCO codes 7*, 8* and 9*
municipalities follow the larger definition of Foged and Peri (2015): 97 aggregated municipalities less 3 excluded, i.e. 94

the instrument (equation 2) combines national immigrant inflows by country of origin relative to 1993 with each municipality's 1993 share of migrants from that country; 142 countries of origin, 3,497 shocks, 25 periods (Table A.8)
because the shares are incomplete, all IV regressions control for the local 1993 immigrant population share interacted with year fixed effects
capital stock is total fixed assets minus the value of industrial robots at the firm level
standard errors are clustered at the municipality level (for multi-establishment companies, the municipality of the establishment with the largest employment share)

claims.statement: A higher share of non-Western immigrant workers in a Danish municipality is associated with a lower the probability that a firm in that municipality adopts at least one robot (Table 4, column 1: no controls beyond fixed effects).

register_source.value: IDA (Integrated Database for Labor Market Research): individual nationality / country of origin

definition.value: Img^{non-west}_{mt} = F^{non-west}_{mt} / P_{mt}: the stock of immigrant workers of non-Western origin divided by total employment in municipality m and year t; a share between 0 and 1, measured at the municipality (not firm) level

register_source.value: Foreign Trade Statistics Register (Statistics Denmark), linked to FIRM and IDA via FIDA

definition.value: binary variable equal to 1 if the firm imports at least one robot in year t; robots are defined by the Harmonized System product codes 847950 (industrial robots) and 847989 (other machines and mechanical appliances having individual functions)

timing.value: firm i, same year t as the immigrant share

units.value: change in the probability that a firm adopts at least one robot in year t (0-1 scale) per one-unit (i.e. 100 percentage point) increase in the municipality's non-Western immigrant share; a one percentage point increase is one hundredth of the printed coefficient

magnitude.interpretation: 'a one percentage point increase in our share variable associates with a 0.003 decrease in the probability of robot adoption, which is equivalent to a 7% decline'

estimand.target_population: Danish private-sector firms with more than 50 employees located in 94 municipalities, 1995-2019
estimand.time_horizon: contemporaneous: the municipality immigrant share and the firm outcome are both measured in year t; no lag structure is imposed

population.description: Danish private-sector firms with more than 50 employees that are active for at least 12 years, 1995-2019, linked to their workers and located in 94 municipalities
population.region: Denmark (94 municipalities, the 97 aggregated municipalities of Foged and Peri (2015) less 3 that never had a robot adoption)
population.selection: firms in the Firm Statistics Register (FIRM); wholesale machinery firms, robot integrators, robot exporters, firms with fewer than 50 employees, firms lasting less than 12 years and 3 outlier municipalities are dropped in that order (Table A.1), leaving 61,007 firm-year observations

identification.source_of_variation: time and geographic variation in the share of non-Western migrant workers across 94 Danish municipalities 1995-2019, driven by political turmoil and wars abroad and by the Danish Refugee Spatial Dispersal Policy, which until the mid-1990s allocated refugees to municipalities without regard to their characteristics or local economic conditions

key_assumptions.assumption: Conditional ignorability: given firm, 2-digit industry and year fixed effects, the municipality non-Western immigrant share is unrelated to unobserved determinants of firm robot adoption
key_assumptions.supported_by: the paper argues this assumption fails and that the OLS estimate is biased towards zero: 'the OLS estimations suffer from spurious positive bias'

lhs: Non-West Immigrant Share
rhs: Unobserved municipality-level shocks affecting both immigration and robot adoption

implies_edges.from: Unobserved municipality-level shocks affecting both immigration and robot adoption

threats_discussed: municipality-specific shocks that drive both immigration and robot adoption (addressed with the shift-share IV)
municipalities with many successful firms able to invest in automation may also attract immigrants - a positive bias on the OLS coefficient
endogeneity of the firm and workforce controls themselves (results shown with and without them, and with base-year values)

robot imports are a proxy for adoption: distributors, robot integrators and robot exporters generate false positives; firms buying from domestic integrators generate false negatives (false-positive rate 4.7%, false-negative rate 70.6% against the VITA survey)
serial correlation of immigrant flows may violate the exclusion restriction (Jaeger et al., 2018)
non-experimental variation from incomplete shares (Borusyak et al., 2022), handled by controlling for the 1993 immigrant population share interacted with year
robustness_checks: alternative robot-adoption measures: narrow HS code, occupation-based, VITA-validated, first-time adopters, intensive margin (Table 5)
placebo outcomes: imports of non-automation machines and the firm capital stock (Table 5, columns 5-6)
excluding postal codes hosting robot integrators and distributors (Table 5, column 7)
alternative immigration measures: refugees, non-refugee non-Western, Western, 1993-1999 base shares, firm-level share (Table 6)
including small firms and short-duration firms; quadratic in the immigrant share; excluding movers, industry switchers and Copenhagen; coarser commuting zones; lagged controls (Table A.3)
alternate firm-identifier sample that links firms through mergers, divisions and legal-form changes (Table A.4)
pre-sample trend tests of the instrument (Table 3)
Adao, Kolesar and Morales (2019) standard-error correction (Table 4, column 6)
controlling for instrumented lagged immigrant flows following Jaeger et al. (2018) (Appendix A.5.2)
unresolved_confounders: false negatives in the import-based adoption measure: firms that buy robots from domestic integrators or distributors are not observed (false-negative rate 70.6% in the VITA comparison)

the estimate is described as a lower bound because Danish collective agreements set a minimum wage for low-skilled workers and the informal sector is small, and because immigrant employment rates are lower than natives'
the firm and workforce control variables are themselves potentially endogenous

estimator.value: OLS with firm, 2-digit industry and year fixed effects

estimation.specification: equation (1): robot adoption regressed on the municipality non-Western immigrant share with no controls beyond fixed effects
estimation.clustering: robust standard errors clustered at the municipality level (for multi-establishment companies, the municipality of the establishment with the largest employment share)

population.description: Danish private-sector firms with more than 50 employees that are active for at least 12 years, 1995-2019, linked to their workers and located in 94 municipalities

identification.source_of_variation: time and geographic variation in the share of non-Western migrant workers across 94 Danish municipalities 1995-2019, driven by political turmoil and wars abroad and by the Danish Refugee Spatial Dispersal Policy, which until the mid-1990s allocated refugees to municipalities without regard to their characteristics or local economic conditions

key_assumptions.supported_by: Fig. 4 scatter of realized against predicted share; first-stage F-statistics and the identification-robust Anderson-Rubin Wald test reported at the bottom of every IV column

implies_edges.from: Shift-share predicted non-Western immigrant share, Img IV^{non-west}_{mt} = sum_d (F_dt / F_d93) * (F_md93 / P_m93)

key_assumptions.assumption: Shifter exogeneity: the country-of-origin immigrant inflows (shifters) are as-good-as-randomly assigned - large in number, not concentrated, and driven by push factors abroad - so they are independent of unobserved municipality shocks once year effects and the 1993 immigrant share interacted with year are controlled for
key_assumptions.supported_by: 142 country-of-origin shifters, none dominant (Table A.8); push-factor test following Ortega and Peri (2009) in Appendix A.5.1; the 1993 shares pre-date widespread robot use and about half the immigrant population was allocated by the Danish Spatial Dispersal Policy

lhs: Shift-share predicted non-Western immigrant share, Img IV^{non-west}_{mt} = sum_d (F_dt / F_d93) * (F_md93 / P_m93)

implies_edges.to: Shift-share predicted non-Western immigrant share, Img IV^{non-west}_{mt} = sum_d (F_dt / F_d93) * (F_md93 / P_m93)

key_assumptions.assumption: No interference across municipalities: native relocation to other municipalities and sectors in response to immigration has a minimal net effect on local labor supply, so one municipality's immigrant share does not affect robot adoption elsewhere
key_assumptions.supported_by: asserted in the hypothesis section; the paper also notes Danish municipalities approximate commuting zones, with only 10% of job changers moving municipality

implies_edges.from: Non-Western immigrant share in other Danish municipalities

threats_discussed: municipality-specific shocks that drive both immigration and robot adoption (addressed with the shift-share IV)
municipalities with many successful firms able to invest in automation may also attract immigrants - a positive bias on the OLS coefficient
endogeneity of the firm and workforce controls themselves (results shown with and without them, and with base-year values)

robot imports are a proxy for adoption: distributors, robot integrators and robot exporters generate false positives; firms buying from domestic integrators generate false negatives (false-positive rate 4.7%, false-negative rate 70.6% against the VITA survey)
serial correlation of immigrant flows may violate the exclusion restriction (Jaeger et al., 2018)
non-experimental variation from incomplete shares (Borusyak et al., 2022), handled by controlling for the 1993 immigrant population share interacted with year
robustness_checks: alternative robot-adoption measures: narrow HS code, occupation-based, VITA-validated, first-time adopters, intensive margin (Table 5)
placebo outcomes: imports of non-automation machines and the firm capital stock (Table 5, columns 5-6)
excluding postal codes hosting robot integrators and distributors (Table 5, column 7)
alternative immigration measures: refugees, non-refugee non-Western, Western, 1993-1999 base shares, firm-level share (Table 6)
including small firms and short-duration firms; quadratic in the immigrant share; excluding movers, industry switchers and Copenhagen; coarser commuting zones; lagged controls (Table A.3)
alternate firm-identifier sample that links firms through mergers, divisions and legal-form changes (Table A.4)
pre-sample trend tests of the instrument (Table 3)
Adao, Kolesar and Morales (2019) standard-error correction (Table 4, column 6)
controlling for instrumented lagged immigrant flows following Jaeger et al. (2018) (Appendix A.5.2)
unresolved_confounders: false negatives in the import-based adoption measure: firms that buy robots from domestic integrators or distributors are not observed (false-negative rate 70.6% in the VITA comparison)

the estimate is described as a lower bound because Danish collective agreements set a minimum wage for low-skilled workers and the informal sector is small, and because immigrant employment rates are lower than natives'
the firm and workforce control variables are themselves potentially endogenous

identification.instrument: Shift-share predicted non-Western immigrant share, Img IV^{non-west}_{mt} = sum_d (F_dt / F_d93) * (F_md93 / P_m93)

key_assumptions.assumption: Exclusion restriction: the shift-share predicted immigrant share affects firm robot adoption only through the actual municipality share of non-Western workers
key_assumptions.supported_by: the paper defends it indirectly: Table 3 shows the long-run change in the instrument is uncorrelated with pre-sample trends in robot use, imports, exports, capital stock and the low-skill share; Appendix A.5.2 re-estimates controlling for instrumented lagged immigrant flows (Jaeger et al., 2018)

implies_edges.from: Shift-share predicted non-Western immigrant share, Img IV^{non-west}_{mt} = sum_d (F_dt / F_d93) * (F_md93 / P_m93)

key_assumptions.assumption: Instrument relevance: the predicted (shift-share) share strongly predicts the realized municipality share of non-Western workers
key_assumptions.supported_by: Fig. 4 scatter of realized against predicted share; first-stage F-statistics and the identification-robust Anderson-Rubin Wald test reported at the bottom of every IV column

implies_edges.from: Shift-share predicted non-Western immigrant share, Img IV^{non-west}_{mt} = sum_d (F_dt / F_d93) * (F_md93 / P_m93)

key_assumptions.assumption: Shifter exogeneity: the country-of-origin immigrant inflows (shifters) are as-good-as-randomly assigned - large in number, not concentrated, and driven by push factors abroad - so they are independent of unobserved municipality shocks once year effects and the 1993 immigrant share interacted with year are controlled for
key_assumptions.supported_by: 142 country-of-origin shifters, none dominant (Table A.8); push-factor test following Ortega and Peri (2009) in Appendix A.5.1; the 1993 shares pre-date widespread robot use and about half the immigrant population was allocated by the Danish Spatial Dispersal Policy

threats_discussed: municipality-specific shocks that drive both immigration and robot adoption (addressed with the shift-share IV)
municipalities with many successful firms able to invest in automation may also attract immigrants - a positive bias on the OLS coefficient
endogeneity of the firm and workforce controls themselves (results shown with and without them, and with base-year values)

robot imports are a proxy for adoption: distributors, robot integrators and robot exporters generate false positives; firms buying from domestic integrators generate false negatives (false-positive rate 4.7%, false-negative rate 70.6% against the VITA survey)
serial correlation of immigrant flows may violate the exclusion restriction (Jaeger et al., 2018)
non-experimental variation from incomplete shares (Borusyak et al., 2022), handled by controlling for the 1993 immigrant population share interacted with year
robustness_checks: alternative robot-adoption measures: narrow HS code, occupation-based, VITA-validated, first-time adopters, intensive margin (Table 5)
placebo outcomes: imports of non-automation machines and the firm capital stock (Table 5, columns 5-6)
excluding postal codes hosting robot integrators and distributors (Table 5, column 7)
alternative immigration measures: refugees, non-refugee non-Western, Western, 1993-1999 base shares, firm-level share (Table 6)
including small firms and short-duration firms; quadratic in the immigrant share; excluding movers, industry switchers and Copenhagen; coarser commuting zones; lagged controls (Table A.3)
alternate firm-identifier sample that links firms through mergers, divisions and legal-form changes (Table A.4)
pre-sample trend tests of the instrument (Table 3)
Adao, Kolesar and Morales (2019) standard-error correction (Table 4, column 6)
controlling for instrumented lagged immigrant flows following Jaeger et al. (2018) (Appendix A.5.2)
unresolved_confounders: false negatives in the import-based adoption measure: firms that buy robots from domestic integrators or distributors are not observed (false-negative rate 70.6% in the VITA comparison)

the estimate is described as a lower bound because Danish collective agreements set a minimum wage for low-skilled workers and the informal sector is small, and because immigrant employment rates are lower than natives'
the firm and workforce control variables are themselves potentially endogenous
